newsitem.title: UK: National Power's U.K. Orimulsion plan gets boost.
newsitem.headline: National Power's U.K. Orimulsion plan gets boost.

text.p: National Power Plc's bid to burn Orimulsion at its Pembroke power station in south Wales was boosted on Thursday after the local county council approved key development proposals.

The British power generator's plans to convert the power station to burn the Venezuelan fuel -- a mixture of bitumen and water once dubbed the "world's filthiest" -- have been dogged by delays in planning permission sparked mainly by environmental concerns.

Pembrokeshire County Council approved the revised proposal -- which includes the modification of an existing jetty at the plant as well as the replacement of a pipeline to a nearby Texaco refinery -- by 15 votes to three.
The final decision concerning National Power's use of Orimulsion lies with Britain's Environment Agency and Department of Trade and Industry (DTI).
"The council is a consultee and as such it has approved the plan and asked that the DTI to grant permission for the jetty conversion," said Pembrokeshire County Council spokesman Nigel Watts.
Bitor, the unit of state-run Petroleos de Venezuela (PDVSA) responsible for promoting the use of Orimulsion worldwide, saw the decision as a significant move towards the Pembroke project's fruition.

"Denmark and Canada already recognise the benefits of using Orimulsion. I expect that in the not too distant future Pembroke power station will be burning Orimulsion," said Bitor's regional director Ian Hole.
Environmental group Friends of the Earth, which has campaigned against the use of Orimulsion, said it was disappointed at the decision but that it was not that significant.
"It was as we expected," said Gordon James, a local Friends of the Earth campaigner. "But I think the decision was based more on the need for jobs than environmental concerns."
"I don't think the decision is terribly significant because the application still faces scrutiny by a number of government agencies," he said.

"I'm disappointed about the decision because there was an opportunity to get a public enquiry which is what one in two local people want," he added. "There is a lot of concern in the local community."

"This ruling applies to planning permission and not the use of Orimulsion. That is covered by a separate application," said Catherine Spooner at the Environment Agency's Welsh office. "The final decision is still a long way off." -- Melanie Goodfellow, London Newsroom, +44 171 542 7714
